segments.text: This is a self-hosted Arabic and English retrieval-augmented generation system for an enterprise knowledge bank. It combines hybrid search, two fine-tuned models, and a local language model. Everything you will see runs live, on a single four-gigabyte laptop GPU.

The brief asked for three search modes behind one API: instant keyword search, AI answers with citations, and multi-turn conversation. It had to handle Arabic, English, mixed queries, and cross-lingual questions, where the answer lives in a document written in the other language. Fine-tuning was mandatory, and every model had to be open source and self-hosted.

Here is the Smart Search pipeline. A query is normalised, then searched two ways at once: BM25 over a SQLite full-text index with a custom Arabic analyzer, and dense vector search with a fine-tuned multilingual E5 model in FAISS. The two rankings are merged with weighted reciprocal rank fusion. A fine-tuned cross-encoder reranks the top twenty and keeps the best four. A confidence gate decides whether to answer at all. Then Qwen 3.5, running in llama.cpp, streams an answer whose citations are checked against the sources.

The knowledge bank holds forty-six documents in Arabic, English, and both, as PDF, Word, HTML and Markdown. We wrote four hundred and forty-one evaluation questions, including Saudi dialect, unanswerable questions, and full conversations, and split them by document, so the test set only contains documents the models never saw in training. Arabic needed real engineering: unifying letter variants, removing diacritics, light stemming, and repairing Arabic PDFs, whose text comes out reversed and broken from standard extractors.

Why hybrid search? Keyword search is precise for names, codes and numbers, but blind across languages. Dense search understands meaning across languages, but can miss exact terms. Reciprocal rank fusion combines them using ranks instead of raw scores: each passage scores the sum of a weight divided by k plus its rank. Both k and the dense weight were tuned on the validation set only.

The first fine-tuned model is the embedder, multilingual E5 base. It is trained contrastively: each question is pulled toward its correct passage, and pushed away from every other passage in the batch, plus hard negatives mined from the training documents, with a margin filter that removes false negatives. To fit a large batch into four gigabytes, we used gradient caching and froze the word embeddings. Every answer was also reused as a question in the other language, to teach cross-lingual matching. Validation nDCG at ten rose from 0.66 to 0.89, in under ten minutes of training.

The second model is the reranker, a multilingual GTE cross-encoder that reads the question and the passage together. The first training runs collapsed: validation MRR fell from 0.88 to 0.15. We isolated the cause step by step. The forward pass was correct, gradients were healthy in an overfitting test, and a smaller control model trained fine on the same data. The fix was a much lower learning rate in full precision, plus denoised negatives. The selected run reached 0.94, picked automatically on validation.

Reliability matters as much as accuracy. The reranker's top score feeds a confidence gate, calibrated on validation for each model, so the system says not found instead of guessing. The prompt only allows facts from the sources, every citation is verified, and refusals phrased in the model's own words are caught and replaced with one clear message.

Running it needs no Docker: one script per step. Set up the environment, prepare the data, build the indexes, fine-tune, and start everything with a single command. The API and the web interface then run on port 8010.
Here is the live system. The API exposes one search endpoint for all three modes, plus document ingestion, sessions, and a health check.
Quick Search is pure BM25. It is instant, runs on the CPU, and understands Arabic word forms, here for installation fees, and English, here for the warranty period.
Smart AI Search, in Arabic. The answer streams in, written only from the knowledge bank, and the numbered citation points to its source passage on the right.
In English, with prices and durations: shipping to Kuwait. Every number comes from the shipping policy, and the bar underneath shows where each millisecond went.
Mixed Arabic and English: a Saudi dialect question about enterprise pricing, then Arabic with an English product name.
A cross-lingual question: asked in Arabic, answered from an English expense policy, and replied to in Arabic.
A long question with several conditions gets one complete answer. And when the documents do not contain the answer, the system says so, instead of inventing one.

Interactive mode keeps a memory of the conversation. The follow-up only makes sense with the previous turn, so it is rewritten into a standalone question first. Switching to English in the middle still works.

Now the effect of fine-tuning, live. The same question goes to the original models on the left and the fine-tuned models on the right. It is asked in Arabic, but the answer is in an English report. The original models find only unrelated Arabic documents, and would answer not found. After fine-tuning, the right English document ranks first.

Across one hundred and thirty-eight held-out test questions, fine-tuning raised top-five retrieval from 85 to 92 percent, and cross-lingual retrieval from 68 to 91 percent. Wrong not-found answers fell from 28 to 17 percent, and hallucinations from 9 to 6 percent. One honest caveat: same-language Arabic retrieval dipped by one question, and that is documented.
On this laptop GPU, the first words of an answer arrive after about 0.4 seconds, Quick Search answers in about a millisecond, and the API served up to sixteen parallel users with no failed requests.
The code, data, benchmarks, error analysis and known limitations are all documented in the repository, and both fine-tuned models are published on Hugging Face. Thank you for watching.
